title: Machiavelli's Prince
objective: After this level you can explain why Machiavelli advised rulers that it can be safer to be feared than loved, and why his name became an insult.
summary: Machiavelli’s Prince (1513) says a ruler is safer feared than loved, never hated, and must be lion and fox; Strauss called him a teacher of evil, Skinner read him more mildly.

cards.headline: A book written to win back a job made its author’s name an insult.
cards.body: Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513, out of office and hoping for work. Today “Machiavellian” means cunning and duplicitous. What did he say that stuck so hard?

cards.headline: Written in disgrace
cards.body: When the Medici family took back Florence, Machiavelli lost his government post. Wrongly suspected of plotting against them, he was jailed and tortured in early 1513. Later that year he wrote The Prince, a short book of advice for rulers, partly to win back his place in politics. It was only published in 1532, after his death.

cards.headline: Better feared than loved
cards.body: Is it better to be loved or feared? Ideally both, Machiavelli says, but since that’s hard, it is much safer to be feared. His reason is a bleak view of people: they are fickle, so love is a bond they break whenever it suits them, while fear holds them by a dread of punishment that never fails. One limit: never be hated, so keep your hands off your subjects’ property.

cards.headline: The lion and the fox
cards.body: A prince needs two animals. The lion can’t defend itself against traps, and the fox can’t defend itself against wolves, so be a fox to spot the traps and a lion to scare the wolves. Machiavelli set aside imagined republics that have “never been known or seen” to write about how people actually live. That was a direct challenge to ideal cities like Plato’s.

cards.headline: Teacher of evil?
cards.body: Sixteenth-century critics denounced him as an apostle of the Devil. In 1958 Leo Strauss called him a “teacher of evil.” Quentin Skinner (1978) read him more mildly, stressing his advice that a prince should do good if he can, and turn to evil only if compelled. Both readings start from the same sentences.

cards.headline: Machiavelli’s Prince: the big picture
learned: Safer to be feared than loved, never hated
Strauss: teacher of evil; Skinner: evil only if compelled

questions.prompt: If a prince can’t have both his people’s love and their fear, Machiavelli says being _____ is safer.

options.label: loved
options.rationale: He says love is broken when it suits people.

options.label: pitied
options.rationale: Pity isn’t one of his options.

options.label: ignored
options.rationale: He wants a prince to be respected, not overlooked.

questions.explanation: Machiavelli says it is much safer to be feared than loved, provided the prince avoids being hated.

questions.prompt: Put these events in Machiavelli’s story in order, from first to last.
questions.explanation: Machiavelli was jailed and tortured in early 1513, wrote The Prince later that year, and the book was only published in 1532, after his death.

questions.prompt: Machiavelli challenged ideal cities like the one in Plato’s Republic. Who did Plato say should rule it?

options.label: Generals
options.rationale: Auxiliaries defend the city; they don’t rule it.

options.label: Merchants
options.rationale: Producers make what the city needs.

options.label: The whole citizen body
options.rationale: Plato’s ship parable argues against rule by the untrained crowd.

questions.explanation: Plato said cities will have no rest from their evils until philosophers become kings.
